rationale: Clinical literature confirms that microcephaly (HP:0000252), particularly postnatal microcephaly, is a bona fide component of the FBXO11-related neurodevelopmental disorder (IDDFBA; OMIM #618089) spectrum. Multiple independent reports document individuals with pathogenic de novo FBXO11 variants presenting with true microcephaly or borderline small head circumference alongside developmental delay, intellectual disability, and behavioral anomalies. Consequently, the presence of microcephaly cannot be used as an exclusionary negative discriminator against FBXO11-related disorder, refuting any notion that microcephaly is strictly absent in this condition. Head circumference in FBXO11-related disease is heterogeneous, ranging from microcephaly to normal to macrocephaly.

evidence.text: Fritzen et al. (2018) describe two unrelated individuals with de novo FBXO11 mutations presenting with ID, behavioral anomalies, and postnatal microcephaly (or borderline small head circumference), and cite an additional literature case sharing the same mutation and microcephaly.

conflicts: Cranial circumference in FBXO11 deficiency is heterogeneous: while multiple studies demonstrate true postnatal microcephaly in ~20-25% of cases, other patients display normocephaly or macrocephaly/increased head circumference, meaning head circumference alone lacks directional specificity.

new_directions.question_text: Do truncating/loss-of-function FBXO11 mutations correlate with microcephaly whereas specific missense mutations or gain-of-function variants associate with normal or macrocephalic head circumference?
new_directions.rationale: Determining genotype-phenotype correlations between mutation class/domain location and cranial biometry will clarify why a quarter develop microcephaly while others have normal or increased head circumference.

new_directions.question_text: Is microcephaly in FBXO11 deficiency predominantly postnatal/secondary due to brain growth deceleration or congenital/primary?
new_directions.rationale: Serial head circumference measurements from birth through adolescence across pooled international registries will determine the exact developmental trajectory of microcephaly in affected individuals.
